results.name: single_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose set has exactly one example (target different from it); observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly from a single example, below means too broadly.

results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and yes (0/1) across all trials; the model has no session dynamics, so observed away from null means people drift toward more yes (positive) or more no (negative) as the session proceeds.

results.name: set_size_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on the number of examples (1-4), over targets not among the examples; observed more negative than null means people tighten generalization with more examples faster than the single evidence-strength model predicts (less negative = slower).
results.code:
# name: set_size_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on the number of examples (1-4), over targets not among the examples; observed more negative than null means people tighten generalization with more examples faster than the single evidence-strength model predicts (less negative = slower).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1).to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    ok = ~s.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1).to_numpy()
    x, y = n[ok], df["rating"].to_numpy(float)[ok]
    if len(x) < 3 or np.var(x) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.cov(x, y, bias=True)[0, 1] / np.var(x))

results.name: shared_last_digit_bonus
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all share a last digit, yes-rate for (non-member) targets with that last digit minus yes-rate for targets without it; observed above null means the model under-weights the "ends in d" rule relative to people.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_bonus
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all share a last digit, yes-rate for (non-member) targets with that last digit minus yes-rate for targets without it; observed above null means the model under-weights the "ends in d" rule relative to people.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    ld = s.mod(10)
    first = ld[0]
    same = ld.eq(first, axis=0) | ld.isna()
    uni = same.all(axis=1) & (n >= 2) & ~s.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    match = uni & (t % 10 == first)
    miss = uni & (t % 10 != first)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    if not match.any() or not miss.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[match].mean() - r[miss].mean())

results.name: inside_vs_outside_range_gap
results.description: Among sets with >=2 examples and targets not in the set, yes-rate for targets inside [min,max] of the examples minus yes-rate for targets outside; observed > null means the model under-produces the interval-like "fill in the range, reject beyond it" contrast.
results.code:
# name: inside_vs_outside_range_gap
# description: Among sets with >=2 examples and targets not in the set, yes-rate for targets inside [min,max] of the examples minus yes-rate for targets outside; observed > null means the model under-produces the interval-like "fill in the range, reject beyond it" contrast.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    mn, mx = s.min(axis=1), s.max(axis=1)
    member = s.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    ok = (n >= 2) & ~member
    inside = ok & (t >= mn) & (t <= mx)
    outside = ok & ((t < mn) | (t > mx))
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    a = r[inside].mean() if inside.any() else 0.5
    b = r[outside].mean() if outside.any() else 0.5
    return float(a - b)

results.name: parity_match_gap
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that are all even or all odd but do NOT share a last digit, yes-rate for non-member targets of the same parity minus targets of opposite parity; observed above null means people use the parity (even/odd) rule more than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_gap
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that are all even or all odd but do NOT share a last digit, yes-rate for non-member targets of the same parity minus targets of opposite parity; observed above null means people use the parity (even/odd) rule more than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    par = s.mod(2)
    p0 = par[0]
    samepar = (par.eq(p0, axis=0) | par.isna()).all(axis=1)
    ld = s.mod(10)
    sameld = (ld.eq(ld[0], axis=0) | ld.isna()).all(axis=1)
    ok = samepar & ~sameld & (n >= 2) & ~s.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    match = ok & (t % 2 == p0)
    miss = ok & (t % 2 != p0)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    if not match.any() or not miss.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[match].mean() - r[miss].mean())

results.name: outside_distance_slope
results.description: For targets outside the examples' [min,max] range, OLS slope of yes (0/1) on log(1 + distance to the nearest example); a more negative observed than null means people's generalization falls off with distance more steeply than the model predicts (less negative = flatter).
results.code:
# name: outside_distance_slope
# description: For targets outside the examples' [min,max] range, OLS slope of yes (0/1) on log(1 + distance to the nearest example); a more negative observed than null means people's generalization falls off with distance more steeply than the model predicts (less negative = flatter).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    mn, mx = s.min(axis=1), s.max(axis=1)
    out = (t < mn) | (t > mx)
    d = s.sub(t, axis=0).abs().min(axis=1)
    x = np.log1p(d[out].to_numpy(float))
    y = df["rating"][out].to_numpy(float)
    if len(x) < 3 or np.var(x) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.cov(x, y, bias=True)[0, 1] / np.var(x))

results.name: recency_last_example_gap
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples and non-member targets, yes-rate when the target is strictly closer to the last-shown example than to the first-shown one minus the reverse; the model is order-invariant, so observed above null means a recency (last-example) weighting the model lacks, below means primacy.
results.code:
# name: recency_last_example_gap
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples and non-member targets, yes-rate when the target is strictly closer to the last-shown example than to the first-shown one minus the reverse; the model is order-invariant, so observed above null means a recency (last-example) weighting the model lacks, below means primacy.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    arr = s.to_numpy(float)
    last = arr[np.arange(len(arr)), (n.to_numpy() - 1)]
    first = arr[:, 0]
    tv = t.to_numpy(float)
    dl, dfst = np.abs(tv - last), np.abs(tv - first)
    ok = (n.to_numpy() >= 2) & ~s.eq(t, axis=0).any(axis=1).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    a, b = ok & (dl < dfst), ok & (dfst < dl)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
